name: pe.ayni.AyniApplication
comment:
Entry point of the Ayni modular monolith.

Each package directly under {@code pe.ayni} is an application module owning its own database schema. Modules do not import one another: they either publish a domain event, or expose an interface at their own root package for others to call.

{@code config} and {@code shared} are declared as shared packages because they hold cross cutting wiring and building blocks rather than business capability, so any module may use them.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingApi
comment:
What booking offers to the other modules.

Implemented by a class in {@code booking.application}.

methods.name: requireBooking
methods.comment: @throws java.util.NoSuchElementException when the booking does not exist in the current tenant

methods.name: openHoursOf
methods.comment:
The tutor's hours in the current university that have not started at {@code from} and can still be booked, earliest first.

Added for matching, which keeps its search projection from events and needs to ask which hours a tutor already has when a course is enabled after they were generated, or when a cancellation gives hours back. An hour somebody holds counts as open: a hold lasts five minutes and ends either in a booking, which is announced, or back in circulation, which is not.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingStatus
comment: Lifecycle of a booking.

name: pe.ayni.booking.BookingView
comment: A booking as the other modules see it.

name: pe.ayni.booking.OpenHourView
comment:
One of a tutor's hours that can still be booked, as the other modules see it.

Carries only what a reader outside booking can act on: which block, and when. Who holds it and why it is free stay inside booking, which decides at confirmation whether it still is.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.AddAvailabilityExceptionUseCase
comment:
Records that one date does not look like the tutor's usual week.

Whether the times are allowed is the entity's business, not this one's: passing a start with no end is refused where the rule lives, which is also where the database enforces it.

The hours of that date usually exist already, so the change reaches them in the same transaction through {@link HourBlockHorizon#adjustFor}: a REMOVE withdraws the hours it takes away, and an ADD generates the ones it gives, so both can be found, or stop being found, as soon as the tutor saves them. Booked hours stand.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.AddAvailabilityPauseUseCase
comment:
Takes a tutor out of circulation for a stretch of days.

Two pauses that overlap would say the same thing twice and make the second one impossible to cancel meaningfully, so the overlap is refused. That check stays in the query: it is a range test the index answers directly, and unlike the weekly windows there is no second copy of it in the entity to drift from.

The hours of those days usually exist already, generated weeks ahead, so saving the pause is not enough: {@link HourBlockHorizon#adjustFor} withdraws them in the same transaction, and a pause that could not be saved withdraws nothing. Booked hours in the pause stand.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: @throws BookingRuleViolation when the pause is backwards or runs into one already recorded

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.BookHoursUseCase
comment:
US03: a student books the hours they are holding.

The confirmation itself is {@link ConfirmBooking}, one transaction. This class has none on purpose, because what it does happens after that transaction is over: when the confirmation fails, it rolls back whole, so the balance is as it was, and then a second transaction gives back the hours the student was holding, so they return to the search at once instead of five minutes later. Doing that inside the failed transaction is impossible: the refusal has already marked it for rollback.

methods.name: giveBackHeldHours
methods.comment:
Releases what the student held in that stretch, in a transaction of its own.

A failure here must not hide the one that brought us here: it is attached to it and the holds are left to run out on their own.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.BookingFailed
comment:
A confirmation that failed for a reason nobody refused on purpose: a database error, a bug.

By the time this is thrown the confirmation's transaction has rolled back, so nothing was charged, and the student's holds have been dealt with. The message says both, because a student who sees an error while paying wants to know first whether they paid.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.BookingService
comment:
What the other modules see of booking.

Sessions keeps only the booking's id; the need description, which the tutor reads before the session and the support material will be generated from, is read through here rather than copied into every module that wants it.

Matching asks here which hours a tutor still has open, because its search is a projection fed by events and an event only tells it about hours at the moment they appear.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.ConfirmBooking
comment:
The confirmation, in the order the backend guide gives it, inside one transaction: the tutor is enabled, the hours are consecutive and free, charge the credits, mark the hours, save the booking, publish {@code BookingConfirmed}. If anything fails, nothing happened.

Nothing here catches anything. Wallet's charge runs inside this transaction and a refusal from it marks the transaction for rollback; catching it here and carrying on would end in a commit that fails with {@code UnexpectedRollbackException}. Refusals leave this class as they are, the transaction rolls back whole, and {@link BookHoursUseCase} deals with the aftermath outside it.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.ConfirmedBooking
comment: A booking just confirmed: what it covers, what it cost, and the hours it took.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.DeclareWeeklyAvailabilityUseCase
comment:
Declares one of a tutor's weekly windows.

A tutor cannot be free twice over the same hour, so the window is refused when it runs into one they already have. Whether it does is {@link AvailabilityPattern#overlaps}: the repository brings back that weekday's windows and the entity decides, rather than the rule being written a second time in SQL where nobody would see it change.

methods.name: execute
methods.signature: execute(java.util.UUID, java.time.DayOfWeek, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.LocalDate, java.time.LocalDate)
methods.comment: Saves the window and generates its hours up to the horizon in the same transaction, so they can be found as soon as the tutor saves them (US19, scenario 1). A tutor without an enabled skill keeps the window but gets no hours, and the answer says why (scenario 5).

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.DeclaredAvailability
comment: A weekly window just declared, and the hours its declaration generated.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.DeclaredException
comment: A date exception that was just saved, and what it did to the hours of that date.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.DeclaredPause
comment: A pause that was just saved, and what it did to the hours that already existed.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.GenerateHourBlocksUseCase
comment:
Materialises a tutor's availability into bookable hours.

{@link BlockGenerator} works out which hours the rules produce; this use case loads what it needs, keeps the whole thing in one transaction, writes only the hours that are not there already, and says what appeared.

Running it twice over the same horizon is safe, which matters because availability is regenerated whenever a tutor changes anything and a scheduled job walks the same days again.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: Generates the hours of a tutor between two dates, both included.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HeldHours
comment: Hours a student has just taken out of circulation while they describe what they need.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HoldHoursUseCase
comment:
Takes the hours a student chose out of circulation for five minutes, so nobody else can take them while the student writes what they need help with.

Without it two students can be filling in the same confirmation and one of them loses the booking after having written everything. Two students choosing the same free hour at the same moment is decided by the version column: both read it free, one update finds the version changed and loses.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HourBlockHorizon
comment:
How far ahead a tutor's hours exist: from today to a fixed number of weeks, in the university's own time zone.

Two callers keep it filled. Declaring a weekly window generates its hours at once, so they can be found the moment the tutor saves them; and a nightly job moves the horizon forward for every tutor, so the weeks keep coming without anybody saving again. Generation writes only the hours that do not exist yet, so both can run over the same range.

The day that counts as today is the university's: a block is shown in its local time, and at eight in the evening in Lima it is already tomorrow in UTC.

methods.name: fillFor
methods.comment: Generates the missing hours of one tutor of the current university, up to the horizon.

methods.name: adjustFor
methods.comment:
Brings a tutor's hours between two dates in line with their availability after it changed: withdraws the hours a pause or a removed date takes away, and generates the ones an added date gives.

Only the part of the range inside the horizon is touched. Days already gone have nothing to adjust, and days beyond the horizon have no hours yet: when the nightly job reaches them it generates them from the rules as they are then, pause and exceptions included.

methods.name: fillForCurrentUniversity
methods.comment: Moves the horizon forward for every tutor of the current university with a window still valid.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HoursAdjustment
comment: How a tutor's hours changed after their availability did: what left, what stands, what appeared.

methods.name: none
methods.comment: Nothing to adjust: the change falls outside the hours that exist.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HoursGeneration
comment: What a run of the hour generation did for one tutor.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.HoursWithdrawal
comment: What withdrawing a tutor's hours did.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.ReleaseExpiredHoldsUseCase
comment:
Returns to circulation the holds of the current university whose five minutes ran out.

An expired hold can already be taken over by anybody without waiting for this, so nothing is wrong between the moment a hold dies and the moment this runs. What this adds is that the hour reads as free again, for the tutor's agenda and for whoever looks at it.

methods.name: forCurrentUniversity
methods.comment: One transaction per university: the caller binds one at a time.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.ReleaseHoldsUseCase
comment:
Gives back the hours a student is holding, so they return to the search at once instead of when the hold runs out.

Two moments call it: the student leaving the confirmation, and a confirmation that failed. The second one runs after the failed transaction has already rolled back, in a transaction of its own, which is why a failure never leaves the student's hours held.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: Releases whatever the student holds in that stretch of the tutor's hours. Hours they do not hold are left alone, so asking twice is harmless.

name: pe.ayni.booking.application.WithdrawUnavailableHoursUseCase
comment:
Takes out of circulation the hours a tutor's availability no longer gives (US20, US22).

Hours are generated weeks ahead, so a pause or a removed date usually arrives after the hours it covers already exist. Those hours have to go, or they stay in the search and a student can book the tutor while they are away.

Which hours go is not decided here. {@link BlockGenerator} works out what the tutor's rules produce now, the same way it does when it creates hours, and every future hour that exists and is not among them is withdrawn. Asking the generator rather than writing the rule again for pauses and for exceptions keeps one definition of when a tutor is free; a second one would drift.

A booked hour stands, as US19 scenario 4 says: only cancelling undoes a booking, and cancelling refunds. The answer counts those hours so the tutor knows they still have to be there. Hours that have started are left alone, whatever they are.

{@link HoursWithdrawn} says which hours left, so matching takes them out of the search. Running it twice changes nothing the second time.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: Withdraws the tutor's hours between two dates, both included, that the rules no longer give.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.AvailabilityException
comment:
A date specific deviation from a tutor's recurring availability.
  • REMOVE takes away availability the patterns would otherwise give. Without times it covers the whole day; with them it covers that window.
  • ADD introduces extraordinary availability outside the recurring hours of that date, and always carries times.

Block generation applies these over the patterns before materialising {@code booking.hour_blocks}.

It is not a Java exception despite the name, which is the table's. It is an exception to a schedule.

methods.name: affects
methods.comment:
Whether this exception runs through the given block.

Both sides are half open ranges of minutes past midnight, not {@link LocalTime}: a block starting at 23:00 ends at 24:00, and there is no LocalTime for that.

Overlapping is enough. A tutor who removes half ten to half eleven has said they cannot be there then, and an hour running through the middle of that cannot be offered. An exception covering the whole day affects everything.

methods.name: coversAWindow
methods.comment: Whether this exception is about a window of the day rather than the whole of it.

methods.name: removesTheWholeDay
methods.comment: Whether this is a REMOVE with no times, which takes the whole day away.

methods.name: removeWholeDay
methods.comment: Removes availability for the whole of a date.

methods.name: removeSlot
methods.signature: removeSlot(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.time.LocalDate, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: Removes availability for one window of a date.

methods.name: addSlot
methods.signature: addSlot(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.time.LocalDate, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.LocalTime, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: Adds extraordinary availability to a date.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.AvailabilityPattern
comment:
A tutor's recurring weekly availability window.

Availability belongs to the tutor and never to a skill: being free on Monday at five means being free, and any enabled skill can be taught in that hour. Block generation projects these patterns forward over the calendar to produce {@code booking.hour_blocks}.

methods.name: validateInvariants
methods.comment: The same rules ck_availability_patterns_times enforces in the database.

methods.name: overlaps
methods.comment:
Whether two patterns of the same tutor collide: same weekday, overlapping validity, overlapping hours.

This is the only place the rule is written. The repository narrows the candidates down to the patterns worth comparing, and the comparison itself happens here, where it can be read and tested without a database. A rule expressed twice is a rule that drifts.

Touching at the edges is not colliding: a pattern that ends at five and one that starts at five describe consecutive hours, not the same hour. Dates, on the other hand, are inclusive, so a validity ending on the day another begins does overlap on that day.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.AvailabilityPause
comment:
An extended calendar freeze of a tutor's availability.

Inside this window, from {@code startsOn} through {@code endsOn} and including both, block generation skips the tutor entirely, which takes them out of the search without touching the patterns they will come back to: vacations, exam weeks, a term abroad.

methods.name: validateInvariants
methods.comment: The same rule ck_availability_pauses_dates enforces in the database.

methods.name: includes
methods.comment: Whether the pause covers the given date. A one day pause covers that day.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.Booking
comment:
A reservation of one or more consecutive hours with the same tutor.

It only ever comes into existence confirmed: the credits were charged and the hours were marked in the same transaction that saves it. There is no pending booking, because a booking that might still fail is what the hold on the hours is for.

The price is not a parameter. One credit is one hour, so what a booking charges is decided here from the hours it covers, the same rule {@code ck_bookings_pricing} enforces in the database.

methods.name: confirm
methods.signature: confirm(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, int, java.lang.String, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: A booking over hours that have just been charged and taken.

methods.name: price
methods.comment: What this booking costs: one credit per hour.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.BookingRuleViolation
comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked of it.

Booking throws this instead of {@code IllegalArgumentException} or {@code IllegalStateException} so that its refusals can be told apart from a programming mistake. The two look identical from outside and deserve opposite answers: a refusal is something the caller can act on, a mistake is something somebody has to fix.

A missing argument is not one of these. {@code Objects.requireNonNull} stays where it is, because a null that reached an entity is a bug and not a decision.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.CancelledBy
comment: Who cancelled a booking. {@code SYSTEM} covers a session that ended unverified.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.ExceptionKind
comment: What a date specific exception does to the availability the weekly patterns describe.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.HoldExpired
comment:
The student is not holding the hour they are trying to confirm: their hold ran out, or they never took one.

Confirming requires a live hold because the hold is what guarantees the student that nobody else took the hour while they were writing. Once it is gone that guarantee is gone too, and the honest answer is to choose the hour again.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.HourBlock
comment:
One hour of a tutor's time: the unit the search returns and a booking takes.

One credit equals one hour, so a block is also the unit the ledger is charged in. {@code UNIQUE (tenant_id, tutor_id, starts_at)} is what stops a tutor from being in two places at once, and {@code version} is the optimistic lock that decides between two students confirming the same hour at the same moment: one update finds a changed version and loses.

methods.name: validateInvariants
methods.comment: The same rule ck_hour_blocks_range enforces in the database.

methods.name: hold
methods.comment:
Takes the hour out of circulation while a student decides.

An expired hold can be taken over without waiting for the job that cleans them up, which is what keeps an abandoned screen from blocking an hour until the next sweep.

Holding an hour the student already holds changes nothing, and in particular does not extend it: otherwise a hold could be kept alive for as long as somebody kept asking. @throws HourUnavailable when the hour has started, is booked or withdrawn, or somebody else's hold on it has not run out

methods.name: releaseHoldOf
methods.comment:
Gives the hour back when the student holding it leaves the confirmation, or when their confirmation failed.

Only the student's own hold, alive or not. Somebody else's hold, a booked hour and a free one are left as they are, which makes asking twice harmless.

methods.name: releaseHold
methods.comment:
Returns an expired hold to circulation. This is what the scheduled sweep calls.

A block that is not held is left alone, because a sweep that read a stale list should not turn somebody's confirmed hour back into a free one. A hold that has not run out yet is a refusal: it still belongs to the student holding it. @throws BookingRuleViolation when the hold is still alive

methods.name: checkBookableBy
methods.comment:
Whether this student may confirm this hour now.

Confirming turns the student's hold into a booking, so it needs a hold that belongs to them and has not run out. A free hour is not enough: without the hold nothing guaranteed the student that the hour was still theirs while they were writing. @throws HourUnavailable when the hour has started, is booked or withdrawn, or another student holds it @throws HoldExpired when the student does not hold it, or held it and ran out of time

methods.name: book
methods.comment: Confirms the hour against a booking, turning the student's hold into it.  @throws HourUnavailable when the hour cannot be taken any more @throws HoldExpired when the student is not holding it

methods.name: release
methods.comment: Takes a booked hour out of circulation after the booking over it was cancelled.  @throws BookingRuleViolation when the hour was not booked

methods.name: withdraw
methods.comment:
Takes an hour out of circulation for good because the tutor is no longer free then: they paused or removed that time.

A free hour and a held one are withdrawn. A student holding it is only choosing, and the tutor will not be there; their confirmation is refused as an hour no longer offered. A booked hour stands: a confirmed booking is only undone by cancelling it, which refunds the credits, and removing availability is not a way around that. A released hour is already out.

methods.name: isHoldExpired
methods.comment: Whether this block is held by somebody whose time has run out.

methods.name: isHeldBy
methods.comment: Whether this student holds the hour and their hold has not run out.

methods.name: hasStartedAt
methods.comment: Whether the hour has begun: from that moment it can no longer be held or booked.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.HourBlockStatus
comment: Where a one hour block is in its life.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.HourUnavailable
comment:
The hour cannot be taken: another student holds it, it was booked, it was withdrawn or it has already started.

A refusal about the state of the tutor's agenda rather than about the request, which is why it is told apart from a plain {@link BookingRuleViolation}: the student asked for something reasonable and somebody got there first.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.HoursNotOffered
comment:
The tutor does not offer the hours asked for as one consecutive stretch.

A booking covers consecutive hours with the same tutor. Monday at five and Wednesday at seven are two bookings, and so is a request whose second hour the tutor never published.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.StudentNotActive
comment: The student asking to book is not an active member of their university: their access is still pending, or it was restricted.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.model.TutorNotBookable
comment:
The tutor cannot be booked for that subject: they are not an active member of the university, or they are not enabled to teach it there.

The first step of the confirmation, before anything is charged. A tutor can withdraw a skill or lose it between the search and the confirmation, and the search projection may not know yet.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.services.BlockGenerator
comment:
Turns what a tutor says about their week into the hours a student can actually book.

Three things decide it, in this order: a pause removes whole days, a whole day REMOVE removes one more, and what is left is the weekly patterns for that weekday, minus the windows a REMOVE took away, plus the hours an ADD put in.

Nothing here touches the database or the clock: it is given the rules, the range and the moment, and it answers with the blocks. That is what makes it testable without starting Spring.

methods.name: generate
methods.signature: generate(java.util.List, java.util.List, java.util.List, java.time.LocalDate, java.time.LocalDate, java.time.ZoneId, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: The blocks a tutor's rules produce between two dates, both included.

methods.name: wholeHoursBetween
methods.comment:
The whole hours that fit inside a window, as minutes past midnight.

Minutes rather than {@link LocalTime} arithmetic, and that is not a matter of taste. {@code LocalTime.plusHours} wraps around midnight, so a window ending at 23:00 never reached its end and the loop that walked it never finished.

methods.name: isRemoved
methods.comment:
Whether a REMOVE of that date takes this hour away.

Whole day removals were already dealt with before we got here, so only the timed ones are asked, and each one answers for itself.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.services.BlockGenerator$BlockKey
comment: What {@code uq_hour_blocks_tenant_tutor_start} is unique on.

name: pe.ayni.booking.domain.services.RequestedHours
comment:
The consecutive hours of one tutor a student asked for: a start and how many hours from it.

A booking covers consecutive hours, so the blocks found have to be exactly as many as asked for, the first one has to start where the student said, and each one has to start where the one before it ends. Consecutive is decided on instants, never on {@code LocalTime}: {@code LocalTime.plusHours} wraps around midnight, and a stretch from 23:00 to 01:00 is still two consecutive hours.

Whether each hour can be taken is not decided here but by the block itself, which knows who holds it and until when.

methods.name: endOf
methods.comment:
Where the stretch asked for ends: the first moment after its last hour.

It is what the repository is asked for, half open, so that the blocks of the stretch come back in one query instead of one per hour. @throws BookingRuleViolation when no hours are asked for

methods.name: of
methods.comment: Checks that the blocks found cover the stretch asked for, and nothing else.

methods.name: blocks
methods.comment: The blocks, in the order they happen.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.AvailabilityExceptionRepository
comment:
The date specific deviations from a tutor's patterns.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

methods.name: findWithinHorizon
methods.comment: The exceptions falling on a range of dates, both ends included, for generating blocks.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.AvailabilityPatternRepository
comment:
A tutor's recurring weekly windows.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

methods.name: findActiveInHorizon
methods.comment: The patterns still valid somewhere inside a range of dates, for generating blocks.

methods.name: findTutorsWithAvailabilityFrom
methods.comment: Tutors with a weekly window still valid on or after a date, for the nightly generation.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.AvailabilityPauseRepository
comment:
The periods a tutor is away.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

methods.name: findOverlappingPauses
methods.comment: The pauses touching a range of dates, both ends included, for generating blocks.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.BookingDomainConfig
comment:
Makes this module's domain services injectable without letting Spring into the domain.

Annotating {@link BlockGenerator} with {@code @Component} would be shorter and would put a framework import in {@code domain/services}, where the backend guide keeps the rules free of one. Declaring the bean from infrastructure costs this file and nothing else.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.BookingRepository
comment:
The reservations.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.DemoBookingData
comment:
A tutor with hours to book, so US03 can be tried in {@code dev}.

Bruno, the second student of the other modules' demo data, teaches two courses his grades already justify, and is free every afternoon from three to six, Lima time. Ana, who has credits, can hold one of those hours and book it.

The window ends at six on purpose. With {@code hibernate.jdbc.time_zone} set to UTC, a backend whose JVM runs on Lima time (from the IDE rather than Docker) stores availability times shifted five hours, and a window that crosses midnight UTC once shifted is refused by {@code ends_at_time > starts_at_time}. Until that is fixed, this window works in both.

Everything goes through the real paths: the courses are enabled by academic record through {@link SkillsApi}, and the availability is declared with the use case the tutor's endpoint calls, which generates the hours for the coming weeks. Demonstration data that took a shortcut the application cannot take would prove nothing.

It runs when the application is ready, after every module's {@code ApplicationRunner} has created the university, the students and the catalogue it depends on. It runs once: a second start finds Bruno's skills and windows already there and leaves them alone.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.ExpiredHoldsJob
comment:
Returns expired holds to circulation, one university at a time.

Nobody makes this request, so each university is bound explicitly before anything is read, the same way wallet expires credits and the hour horizon moves forward at night. It runs every minute rather than at night because a hold lasts five minutes.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.HourBlockHorizonJob
comment:
Keeps every tutor's hours a few weeks ahead, one university at a time.

Nobody makes this request, so each university is bound explicitly before anything is read, the same way wallet expires credits at night.

methods.name: moveTheHorizonForward
methods.comment: Every night at two, before the credits expire and long before anybody books.

name: pe.ayni.booking.infrastructure.HourBlockRepository
comment:
The generated hours.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

methods.name: findWithin
methods.comment:
A tutor's hours in a window, from the first moment included to the first moment excluded.

Half open rather than {@code between}, which includes both ends: two windows laid end to end would otherwise both claim the hour on the boundary, and an agenda would show it twice.

methods.name: findOpenFrom
methods.comment:
A tutor's hours from an instant on that can still be booked: free, or held by somebody for the few minutes a hold lasts.

A held hour is included on purpose. It either ends booked, which {@code BookingConfirmed} announces, or goes back to circulation without anybody saying so; leaving it out would make it vanish from the search for good in the second case.

methods.name: findExpiredHolds
methods.comment:
The holds of a university whose time ran out, for the job that returns them to circulation.

Strictly before {@code now}, the same comparison {@link HourBlock#isHoldExpired} makes: a hold is still alive at the very instant it ends. The partial index on {@code held_until} where the status is HELD is what keeps this cheap.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.ApiError
comment: The error shape returned by booking endpoints.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityController
comment:
Tutor availability commands.

The controller only translates HTTP requests into application commands. The tutor is always read from {@link CurrentUser}; it is never accepted in the request body.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityExceptionRequest
comment: Request body for a date-specific ADD or REMOVE exception.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityExceptionResponse
comment: The date-specific availability exception that was created.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityPatternResponse
comment: The recurring weekly availability that was created.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityPauseRequest
comment: Request body for an inclusive availability pause.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.AvailabilityPauseResponse
comment: The inclusive availability pause that was created.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.BookHoursRequest
comment: What the contract asks for to book: tutor, skill, start, hours and need description. The hours must be held by the student making the request.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.BookingController
comment:
Holding hours and booking them.

The controller only translates HTTP into use cases. The student is always read from {@link CurrentUser}, never from the body: an endpoint with no way to name another student cannot hold or book on their behalf.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.BookingExceptionHandler
comment:
Maps booking refusals and invalid HTTP input to the module's common error shape.

400 is for a request that is wrong whatever the state of the world. 409 is for a well formed request that the state of the tutor's agenda refuses: somebody got to the hour first, the hold ran out, the tutor does not offer those hours.

methods.name: handleInsufficientCredits
methods.comment: The balance does not cover the hours. Wallet says how many credits are missing and the student is told that number, so they know what they are short of rather than only that they are.

methods.name: handleNotFound
methods.comment: The subject asked for is not one the student's university can see.

methods.name: handleBookingFailed
methods.comment: A confirmation failed for no reason anybody chose. The use case already rolled it back and gave the holds back, and its message says so; the cause was logged where it happened.

methods.name: handleLostRace
methods.comment: Two requests read the same hour free and this one wrote second: the version column refused it.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.BookingResponse
comment: A confirmed booking.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.DeclareAvailabilityRequest
comment: Request body for a recurring weekly availability range.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.HeldHoursResponse
comment: The hours now held for the student, and until when.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.HoldHoursRequest
comment: The hours a student chose, to take them out of circulation while they confirm.

name: pe.ayni.booking.interfaces.rest.HoursNotice
comment:
The one thing a tutor should know after changing their availability, when there is one.

Booked hours that stand come first: the tutor removed that time and may believe they are free, while a student is still expecting them.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: For a change that can add hours as well as take them away: a date exception.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: For a change that only takes hours away: a pause.

name: pe.ayni.config.CorsConfig
comment:
Lets the web application call the API from the browser.

A browser refuses a request to a different origin unless the server says otherwise, and the web application runs on port 5173 while the API runs on 8080. In development the web application usually goes through the Vite proxy, which makes both look like the same origin, but this keeps direct calls working too.

name: pe.ayni.config.CurrentUserFilter
comment:
Reads who is making the request and binds them for the rest of it.

The companion of {@link TenantFilter}, and the same story: the value arrives in the {@code X-User-Id} header today because there is no sign in yet, and when there is, it comes from a claim of the access token and only this class changes. Everything downstream keeps reading it from {@link CurrentUser}.

A header that is not a UUID is left unbound rather than rejected here. Refusing in a filter would answer in a shape no module controls, and every endpoint that needs a user already fails with {@code MissingUserException}, which each module maps for itself.

Clearing it in a {@code finally} block is not optional. The server reuses threads, so a user left behind would be picked up by the next request, which is another person.

name: pe.ayni.config.OpenApiConfig
comment:
OpenAPI description of the API, served through Swagger UI at {@code /swagger-ui.html}.

The documentation is a deliverable of the course, and it is generated from the controllers, so it stays correct as long as the annotations on them are.

methods.name: requestHeadersCustomizer
methods.comment:
Declares {@code X-Tenant-Id} and {@code X-User-Id} on every operation outside {@code /api/v1/access}.

{@link TenantFilter} and {@link CurrentUserFilter} read those headers, but filters are invisible to springdoc, so unless a controller declares them by hand Swagger UI offers no place to type them and "Try it out" answers 400. Declaring them here once is cheaper than repeating the annotation on every endpoint, and it leaves out the access routes, which are public.

It decides by path and not by controller type because {@code config} must not import the internals of any module. A header an operation already declares is left alone, so the controllers that spell them out keep their own description.

It goes away with TS03: once the session token carries the university and the user, nobody has to type them.

name: pe.ayni.config.TenantFilter
comment:
Reads the university the request belongs to and binds it for the rest of the request.

Right now it arrives in the {@code X-Tenant-Id} header, which Postman and the web application send explicitly. When authentication is added, the same value will come from a claim of the access token and only this class changes: everything downstream keeps reading it from {@link TenantContext}.

Clearing it in a {@code finally} block is not optional. The server reuses threads, so a tenant left behind would be picked up by the next request, from another university.

name: pe.ayni.config.TimeConfig
comment:
The clock the application reads time from.

Every rule that depends on time asks for a {@link Clock} instead of calling {@code Instant.now()}, so that a test can decide what "now" is: credits that expire tomorrow, a cancellation eleven hours before the session. A rule that reads the clock statically can only be tested by waiting.

UTC, because every instant stored and returned by the API is in UTC.

name: pe.ayni.identity.ApprovedCourseView
comment: A course the academic system reports as approved.

name: pe.ayni.identity.CreditPolicyView

What identity offers to the other modules. The only way into this module besides its events.

Implemented by a class in {@code identity.application}.

The courses the academic system reports the student approved, with their grade.

Skills uses it to enable a course automatically when the grade reaches the university's threshold, and to suggest what a student could teach.

methods.name: activeTenantCodes
methods.comment: Codes of every active university. Used by scheduled jobs, which run without a request.

name: pe.ayni.identity.PolicyKind
comment: Whether a credit policy applies to every student or to a targeted group.

comment: A university as the other modules see it.

name: pe.ayni.identity.UserRole
comment: The two kinds of user inside a university. The platform administrator is not one of them.

name: pe.ayni.identity.UserView
comment: A student or coordinator as the other modules see them.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.AccessLinkUrlBuilder
comment:
Builds the URL delivered to the user for a single-use access token.

The URL carries the token and nothing else. The university is read from the link itself when it is confirmed, so the client never declares which university it belongs to, and the link of a platform administrator, who belongs to none, has the same shape as everybody else's.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.AccessTokenGenerator
comment: Generates and hashes secure tokens used by the Identity access flow.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.ConfirmAccessResult
comment: The session a confirmed link opened.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.ConfirmAccessUseCase
comment:
US38: opening the link that arrived by email signs the student in.

The link is found by the hash of its token alone, and the university is the one written on the link when it was requested. The client does not say which university it belongs to: a client that could say so could claim any of them, which is the hole the second iteration closes.

A link works once. Consuming it is a single conditional update, so two confirmations of the same link at the same moment open one session, not two. It is consumed before the session is written and in the same transaction, so a confirmation that fails after consuming it leaves the link as it was.

Only signing in exists today. A link that would activate a new student, or accept a coordinator's invitation, is refused with a message that says so: creating those accounts needs the academic system and is a story of its own.

name: pe.ayni.identity.application.GeneratedAccessToken
comment: A newly generated access token.

name: pe.ayni.identity.domain.model.IdentityRuleViolation
comment: A business rule of the Identity module was violated.

name: pe.ayni.identity.domain.model.Tenant
comment:
A university registered in Ayni.

The tenant owns its institutional email domains and academic rules. An institutional email is matched against those domains before a user has an account.

methods.name: claims
methods.comment:
Whether this university owns the domain of the supplied institutional email.

The comparison is case insensitive. Invalid email values simply do not belong to the university.

name: pe.ayni.identity.domain.model.UserSession
comment:
What a confirmed access link leaves behind: the key a student uses until it expires.

Long lived on purpose, as the data model says: if the session were short, every day would start by waiting for an email. The token is stored hashed for the same reason the link's is, so a leaked table opens nobody's account.

A session belongs to a student or to a platform administrator, never both, which is what {@code ck_identity_user_sessions_subject} enforces. Only students sign in today, so only that constructor exists.

methods.name: isActive
methods.comment: Whether the session still opens the door: not revoked and not expired.

methods.name: revoke
methods.comment: Closes the session before it expires, as signing out does.

name: pe.ayni.identity.infrastructure.AccessLinkRepository
comment:
Single-use access links issued by Identity.

One of the two tables the data model reads without the university: a link is opened before anybody knows which university its owner belongs to, and the link is what says it. The token hash is {@code UNIQUE}, so it finds one link at most.

methods.name: consume
methods.comment:
Marks a link as used, only if nobody used it first and it has not expired.

The condition is checked by the database in the same statement that writes, so of two confirmations of the same link arriving at once exactly one changes the row: the other waits for its lock, finds {@code consumed_at} already set and changes nothing. Reading the link and then saving it would let both read it unused.

name: pe.ayni.identity.infrastructure.DemoIdentityData
comment:
A university and two students to look at while signing in does not exist yet.

The students are the same ones {@code DemoWalletData} gives credits to, so every module's demo data describes the same people. Ana starts at the first onboarding step, and the threshold of 13 lets two of the three courses {@code MockAcademicSystemAdapter} reports be offered. Bruno is past the academic record step of onboarding, with his record imported, which is what lets {@code DemoBookingData} enable him as a tutor so that Ana has somebody to book.

It runs once: a second start finds the rows already there and leaves them alone.

name: pe.ayni.identity.infrastructure.MockAcademicSystemAdapter
comment:
Stands in for the universities' academic systems until Ayni integrates with one.

It is active in every profile, not only in {@code dev}: it is the only implementation of {@link AcademicSystemPort}, and without one the application context does not start, which takes every other module's tests down with it. The first real adapter replaces it.

Every UPC student gets the same record. The course codes are the ones {@code DemoSkillsData} puts in the catalogue, so that offering a course works end to end in {@code dev}: two grades clear the demo threshold and one does not.

name: pe.ayni.identity.infrastructure.TenantRepository
comment:
Universities registered in Ayni.

Tenants are not tenant-scoped themselves: they define the universities available in the platform.

name: pe.ayni.identity.infrastructure.UserSessionRepository
comment:
The sessions opened by confirming an access link.

Like the access links, read without the university: a request that presents a session token does not know its university yet, and the session is what will tell it.

name: pe.ayni.identity.interfaces.rest.AccessController
comment:
Signing in with the institutional email: asking for a link, and opening it.

Neither endpoint needs {@code X-Tenant-Id}. Requesting a link decides the university from the domain of the email, and confirming it reads the university from the link.

name: pe.ayni.identity.interfaces.rest.ConfirmAccessRequest
comment: The token of the link the email carried, and nothing else: the university is read from the link, never declared by the client.

name: pe.ayni.identity.interfaces.rest.ConfirmAccessResponse
comment: The session a confirmed link opened.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.FoundOffer
comment: One hour a student found, with what they need to choose between tutors.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.MatchingEventListeners
comment:
What matching does about things that happened elsewhere: it keeps its search projection in step.

Nobody tells matching to add or remove an offer. Booking announces hours and bookings, skills announces courses, reputation announces ratings, and each of them works without knowing the search exists. Each listener runs after the publisher's transaction commits, so an hour whose generation rolled back is never offered.

Every listener binds the university from the event before doing anything, because it runs outside the request that caused it.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: A course enabled after the tutor's hours exist is offered in the hours they still have open.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: A booked hour is nobody else's to find.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: Only a student's rating of a tutor moves the tutor's standing. A tutor rating a student changes nothing anybody searches by.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.OfferProjection
comment:
Keeps {@code matching.available_offers} in step with what the other modules announce.

One row per hour a tutor is free and per course they are enabled to teach. Availability belongs to the tutor, not to a course, so when either side changes the rows are worked out again from the other: new hours are offered for every enabled course, a newly enabled course for every hour already open.

Every method is safe to run twice. Events are delivered in memory today and will be retried once the publication registry arrives (ADR 0005), and a retry must not duplicate an offer nor fail on one that is already there. Adding writes only the offers that are missing; removing and refreshing are the same whatever the rows were.

The projection is allowed to go stale, because booking checks the hour against its own tables when a student holds it and when they book it. That is why a hold does not remove anything: it lasts five minutes, and ends either in a booking, which is announced, or back in circulation.

methods.name: offerHours
methods.comment: Offers new hours of a tutor for every course they are enabled to teach.

methods.name: offerCourse
methods.comment:
Offers a newly enabled course in every hour the tutor already has open.

Skills is asked again rather than trusting the event: a course withdrawn since it was enabled must not come back because the older event was handled late.

methods.name: offerReleasedHours
methods.comment:
Offers again the hours a cancellation gave back, if booking still has them open.

Booking decides whether a cancelled hour returns to circulation; matching only repeats what booking says, so an hour booking keeps out stays out of the search too.

methods.name: withdrawHours
methods.comment: Stops offering these hours, for every course: they were booked or withdrawn.

methods.name: withdrawCourse
methods.comment: Stops offering a course of a tutor, in every hour.

methods.name: refreshStanding
methods.comment: Copies again the tutor's standing in a course into every offer of that course.

methods.name: offer
methods.comment: Writes the offers of these hours and courses that are not there yet.

methods.name: standingOf
methods.comment: What reputation says of the tutor in the course; a tutor who never taught it has nothing.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.OfferSearch
comment: What a search found.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.OpenHour
comment: An hour of a tutor that matching may offer, whichever way it heard of it: announced by {@code HoursGenerated}, or read from {@code BookingApi.openHoursOf}.

name: pe.ayni.matching.application.SearchOffersUseCase
comment:
US01: the hours a student can book for a course, inside the window they can make.

It answers from the projection alone, never from booking or skills, which is what keeps the search fast however many tutors a course has (TS07). Only hours that have not started come back: the time is read from the injected clock, like every rule that depends on it.

Every tutor free at an hour is returned, the best rated first and new tutors last, and the student chooses. Choosing for them would send every booking to the same few tutors and leave the new ones with nothing, which is why the event storming session rejected it.

When nothing falls inside the window, the closest hours outside it come back instead, with {@link OfferSearch#exactMatch()} false so the client can say the window was empty (scenario 2). That answer is a single page of at most {@code size} hours: paging through "the closest" would only mean moving further from what the student asked for.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.model.AvailableOffer
comment:
One hour a tutor is free, offered for one course they are enabled to teach: what a student finds.

Nothing here is decided by matching. The block and its hour come from booking, the course from skills, the name from identity and the standing from reputation; matching copies them when their events arrive so that a search reads one table and joins nothing. A row that went stale is harmless, because booking checks the hour again when it is held and when it is booked.

{@link Persistable} because the key is assigned, not generated: without it every insert would first read the row to find out whether it exists, which the projection already knows.

methods.name: getEndsAt
methods.comment: When the hour ends. Not stored: every block lasts {@link #BLOCK_LENGTH}.

methods.name: isNewTutor
methods.comment: Whether the tutor is shown as new in this course, with no average.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.model.AvailableOfferId
comment: Identifies one offer: a block of a university, for one of the courses its tutor teaches.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.model.MatchingRuleViolation
comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked of it.

Thrown instead of {@code IllegalArgumentException} so that a search the student can correct, such as a range that ends before it starts, is told apart from a programming mistake and answered with a 400 rather than a 500.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.model.SearchWindow
comment:
The hours a student said they can make: from the first instant included to the last excluded.

Half open, like every range of hours in the application, so two windows laid end to end never both claim the hour on the boundary.

methods.name: distanceTo
methods.comment: How far an hour starting at {@code startsAt} is from this window: zero inside it, otherwise the distance to the edge it fell outside of. That is what "closest" means to a student who asked for Tuesday afternoon, rather than the distance to some arbitrary point of the window.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.model.Standing
comment:
A tutor's standing in one course, as reputation reported it when the offer was written.

Copied rather than looked up, so a search that compares ten tutors does not ask reputation ten times. {@code averageStars} is {@code null} while the tutor has too few ratings to show one: reputation decides that threshold and matching only repeats it.

methods.name: none
methods.comment: A tutor who never taught the course: no average, nothing counted.

methods.name: isNewTutor
methods.comment: Whether the tutor is shown as new: there is no average to show for them.

name: pe.ayni.matching.domain.services.NearestOffers
comment:
What a search answers when nothing falls inside the window: the offers closest to it, on either side, instead of an empty page (US01, scenario 2).

An empty answer leaves a student with an exam on Friday nowhere to go; an hour on Wednesday evening instead of Wednesday afternoon may be exactly what they need.

methods.name: around
methods.comment:
Chooses the {@code limit} offers closest to the window among the candidates before and after it, and returns them in {@linkplain AvailableOffer#SEARCH_ORDER search order}, so the answer reads like any other.

Each side only needs its own {@code limit} closest candidates: nothing further away on that side could make the cut.

name: pe.ayni.matching.infrastructure.AvailableOfferRepository
comment:
The search projection.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

The three search queries share their conditions: one course, hours that have not started, never the student's own. A tutor looking for help in a course they also teach would otherwise find themselves, and booking refuses a tutor their own hours.

methods.name: findWithin
methods.signature: findWithin(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable)
methods.comment: The offers inside a window, in {@link AvailableOffer#SEARCH_ORDER}: by time, then the best rated tutor, with new tutors last. The index on {@code (tenant_id, catalog_item_id, starts_at)} is what keeps this cheap.

methods.name: findClosestBefore
methods.signature: findClosestBefore(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, org.springframework.data.domain.Limit)
methods.comment: The offers closest before a window that have not started, the latest first.

methods.name: findClosestAfter
methods.signature: findClosestAfter(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, org.springframework.data.domain.Limit)
methods.comment: The offers closest after a window that have not started, the earliest first.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndBlockIdIn
methods.comment: The offers already written for these blocks, whatever their course.

methods.name: deleteBlocks
methods.comment: Removes every offer of these blocks, one per course the tutor teaches.

methods.name: deleteSkill
methods.comment: Removes every offer of a tutor for one course.

methods.name: updateStanding
methods.signature: updateStanding(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.math.BigDecimal, int, int)
methods.comment: Rewrites the standing copied into every offer of a tutor for one course.

name: pe.ayni.matching.interfaces.rest.ApiError
comment: The error shape returned by matching endpoints.

name: pe.ayni.matching.interfaces.rest.MatchingExceptionHandler
comment:
Maps the search's refusals and invalid HTTP input to the common error shape: timestamp, status, error, message, path.

Scoped to this module's controller, like every module's handler, so that one module's decision about an exception never answers for another's endpoints.

methods.name: handleNotFound
methods.comment: The university in the header does not exist, so there is no time zone to answer in.

name: pe.ayni.matching.interfaces.rest.OfferSearchResponse
comment:
A page of offers.

Described with its own fields rather than returned as a Spring {@code Page}, whose shape is an implementation detail of the framework, the same way wallet and skills answer their lists.

name: pe.ayni.matching.interfaces.rest.OfferSearchResponse$Offer
comment: One hour a tutor is free for the course.

name: pe.ayni.matching.interfaces.rest.SearchOffersController
comment:
The tutor search.

The controller only translates HTTP into the use case. The student is read from {@link CurrentUser}, so the search can leave out their own hours without taking anybody's id as a parameter.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.AccessLinkEmail
comment:
What the email carrying an access link says.

In Spanish, like everything else the student reads in the web application. It says how long the link lasts, that it works once, and what to do if the student did not ask for it: the three things somebody receiving a key by email needs to know.

methods.name: minutesUntil
methods.comment: Whole minutes, rounded up: a link that lasts nine and a half minutes is not "9 minutes".

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.DeliverAccessLinkUseCase
comment:
US38: the access link reaches the inbox it was asked for.

Identity only keeps the hash of the token, so this email is the one and only copy of the link. The notice is recorded first, then the email is sent, then the outcome is recorded; a failure is written down and never thrown, because the student who asked is told to check their email either way, and an exception here would only be logged by the event infrastructure and forgotten.

A failed access link is not retried: the link is not stored anywhere to retry it with, and it expires in minutes. Asking again issues a new one.

No {@code @Transactional} here on purpose: every write goes through {@link NotificationLog}, which commits it on its own, so the notice is in the database before the email leaves whatever transaction the caller has open. Joining the caller's would roll the notice back with it.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.DeliverPresenceCodeUseCase
comment:
US54: the presence code reaches the participant's institutional mailbox.

Sessions keeps only the hash, so this email is the only copy of the code. The event names the participant, not their address, which is identity's: it is read through {@link IdentityApi}, the one thing this module asks another for.

Delivered like the access link: the notice is recorded first, then the email is sent, then the outcome is recorded, and a failure is written down rather than thrown. The notice keeps the session and the expiry, never the code, so a failed code cannot be retried: there is nothing stored to retry it with, exactly as with an access link.

No {@code @Transactional} here, for the same reason as {@link DeliverAccessLinkUseCase}.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.Email
comment: One plain text email, ready to leave.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.EmailDelivery
comment:
Hands an email to whatever carries it.

A port, so the rules about what a notice says and how its outcome is recorded are tested without a mail server, and so the carrier can change without touching them. Implemented over SMTP in {@code notifications.infrastructure}.

methods.name: send
methods.comment: @throws EmailNotDelivered when the carrier refused the email or could not be reached

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.EmailNotDelivered
comment: The carrier did not take the email. The message says why, and is what the notice records.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.NotificationEventListeners
comment:
What notifications does about things that happened elsewhere: it tells the people concerned.

Nothing depends on this module, as the backend guide says. It reacts to events, and asks identity only for the address of a person an event names. Each listener runs after the publisher's transaction commits, so a link or a code whose transaction rolled back is never sent.

The university is bound from the event before anything is done; it may be none, for a platform administrator.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.NotificationLog
comment:
Writes a notice and its outcome, each in a transaction of its own.

The notice is committed before the email leaves, so a delivery interrupted halfway, the process stopping between sending and recording, still leaves a pending notice behind instead of nothing. Writing it in the caller's transaction would roll it back with everything else.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.application.PresenceCodeEmail
comment:
What the email carrying a presence code says.

In Spanish, like the access link. It says where to type the code, until when, and what happens if nobody does: the participant is in a video call and reads this in a hurry. The code is in the body and not in the subject, which mail servers log.

methods.name: minutesUntil
methods.comment: Whole minutes, rounded up, as for the access link.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.domain.model.Notification
comment:
One notice for one person, and whether it reached them.

It is written before the email leaves and then marked sent or failed, never both, which is what {@code ck_notifications_outcome} enforces. A notice that stays pending is one whose delivery was interrupted, and that has to be visible too: getting in and confirming presence depend on it.

The payload describes the notice without repeating any secret it carried. An access link is delivered and forgotten, exactly as identity keeps only its hash.

methods.name: pending
methods.signature: pending(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, pe.ayni.notifications.domain.model.NotificationKind, java.util.Map, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: A notice about to be delivered.

methods.name: isPending
methods.comment: Whether nobody has recorded yet how the delivery went.

methods.name: markSent
methods.comment: Records that the email left.  @throws IllegalStateException when the outcome was already recorded

methods.name: markFailed
methods.comment: Records why the email did not leave, cut to what the column holds.  @throws IllegalStateException when the outcome was already recorded

name: pe.ayni.notifications.domain.model.NotificationKind
comment: What a notice is about. The same list {@code ck_notifications_kind} accepts, so adding one is a migration as well as a constant.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.infrastructure.NotificationRepository
comment:
The notices and how their delivery went.

Only saved and found by id today: a notice is written and marked by the same flow that created it. Reading a person's own notices, which will filter by the university, arrives with {@code GET /api/v1/notifications}.

name: pe.ayni.notifications.infrastructure.SmtpEmailDelivery
comment: Sends email over SMTP, to whichever server {@code spring.mail.*} names: Mailpit under {@code docker compose}, the university's relay in a deployment.

name: pe.ayni.payments.application.PaymentProvider
comment: Boundary to the payment provider; the current adapter simulates its response.

name: pe.ayni.payments.application.PaymentProviderUnavailable
comment: The provider could not be reached; the outcome of the charge remains unknown.

name: pe.ayni.payments.domain.model.PurchaseLimit

name: pe.ayni.payments.infrastructure.PurchaseLimitLock
comment: Serializes purchases for one student while their monthly allowance is checked and consumed.

name: pe.ayni.payments.infrastructure.SimulatedPaymentProvider
comment: Local payment adapter whose outcome can be switched without changing the payments use case.

name: pe.ayni.reputation.ReputationApi
comment:
What reputation offers to the other modules.

Implemented by a class in {@code reputation.application}.

name: pe.ayni.reputation.application.TutorStandingQuery
comment:
US02: a tutor's standing in one course, as a student comparing tutors sees it.

A tutor who never taught the course has no row in {@code reputation.tutor_standing}: the row appears with the first completed session. That tutor is not missing, they are new, and US02 says a new tutor is shown without an average, the same way the search already shows them. So when there is no row but skills says the tutor may teach the course, the answer is a standing with nothing counted. Only a tutor who is not enabled for the course has no standing to show.

A tutor who taught the course and was later withdrawn from it keeps the standing they earned: the row is history, and history is not erased because the offer ended.

comment:
US11, scenario 3: a session that only one participant, or nobody, ended closes on its own {@link Session#CLOSES_AFTER_END} after the booked hour.

It closes exactly as if both had confirmed: the outcome is the presence check's, and who confirmed the end stays recorded on their participation. Each session is closed in a transaction of its own, locked, so a participant ending it at the same moment closes it once between the two.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.ConfirmPresenceUseCase
comment:
US54, scenarios 2 and 4: a participant types in the code they were emailed.

Only a participant who joined the session can confirm: the code proves they are in the room, and somebody who never entered it is not, whatever their mailbox holds.

A wrong code is refused and still counted. The transaction commits on {@link WrongPresenceCode} for that reason: rolling it back would also roll back the attempt, and the cap of five would never be reached. The code is locked while it is checked, so wrong codes sent at once are counted one after the other.

The session is locked too, the same lock closing takes: a code typed in while the session is being closed either counts before the outcome is decided or finds the session closed, never confirmed after it was judged unconfirmed.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.EndSessionUseCase
comment:
US11: a participant confirms the session is over, and the second confirmation closes it.

The story asks for both to confirm the end before the session is completed. One confirmation is recorded and the session waits for the other; if it never comes, the session closes on its own {@link Session#CLOSES_AFTER_END} after the booked hour, and the record shows who confirmed. Only a participant who joined can confirm, since only they were in the session.

The session is locked while it is ended, so the two confirming at once close it once: without the lock each could see the other's confirmation missing, or both see both and close it twice.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.EndedSession

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.IssuePresenceCodesUseCase
comment:
US54, scenario 1: five minutes into a session each participant gets a six digit code.

Both participants get one, including one who has not joined: whoever is not in the session cannot confirm, and that is what the check is for. Only the hash is stored; the code in clear travels in {@link PresenceCodeIssued}, which notifications emails once this transaction commits, so a code whose check was rolled back is never sent.

Each session is issued in a transaction of its own, so a failure in one does not hold back the codes of the others. The session is locked while it is issued, so a sweep that overlaps with another issues each code once; {@code uq_presence_checks_session_user} stands behind it.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.JoinSessionUseCase
comment:
US08: the student and the tutor meet in the room.

Whether the room is open, and whether this person belongs in it, is the session's to decide. This use case locks the session while it does, records the participant's first arrival, and announces the start when this join is the one that started it.

The session is locked rather than read, because the two participants usually arrive within seconds of each other: without the lock both could find it not started, both start it and {@link SessionStarted} would be published twice.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.PresenceConfirmation

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.PresenceState
comment: The reader's own presence code, without the code: what the screen needs to ask for it, say it expired, or say it is done.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.ScheduleSessionUseCase
comment:
Creates the session of a booking that was just confirmed.

Idempotent, because it runs on an event and an event can arrive twice: a booking that already has its session is left as it is, which is also what {@code UNIQUE (booking_id)} would insist on.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionCloser
comment:
Closes a session and announces how it ended. Shared by the participants closing it and by the job that closes what they left open, so both decide the outcome the same way.

The outcome is the presence check's, not the participants': the session is {@code COMPLETED} only when both proved their presence with the emailed code, and {@code UNVERIFIED} otherwise, including when no code was ever sent because the session ended before its fifth minute. That is what makes the tutor's earned credits mean something.

{@link SessionCompleted} pays the tutor the booked hours; wallet and reputation already listen to it. {@link SessionUnverified} names who did not confirm; wallet refunds the student on it. Both are published inside the caller's transaction and reach their listeners once it commits.

Runs inside the caller's transaction, with the session already locked by the caller.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionDetails
comment: A session as one of its participants sees it before and during it.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionDetailsQuery
comment:
A session, for one of its two participants and nobody else.

The need description stays in booking, which owns it, and is read through {@link BookingApi} rather than copied into sessions: the session keeps only the booking's id, as the booking module already expected.

The room name is not part of the answer. It is what lets anyone into the call, so it is only handed over by joining, inside the window the room is open. Nor is the presence code, which only travels by email: the answer says whether it was sent, until when it can be typed in and whether it was, for the reader alone.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: @throws NoSuchElementException when the session does not exist in the current university @throws NotAParticipant when the reader is neither the student nor the tutor

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionEventListeners
comment:
What sessions does about things that happened elsewhere.

A confirmed booking is what creates a session, as the backend guide says: booking does not know sessions exists, it announces the confirmation and sessions reacts. The listener runs after booking's transaction commits, so a booking that rolled back never gets a session.

It binds the university from the event before doing anything, because it runs outside the request that confirmed the booking.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.application.SessionsService
comment:
What the other modules see of sessions.

The interface was published before anything implemented it, so the first module to inject it would have stopped the application from starting. Recognition is that module: a request is backed by the sessions a tutor completed.

Only {@link SessionStatus#COMPLETED} counts as completed. An {@code UNVERIFIED} session took place but failed the presence check, and the backend guide is explicit that it earns the tutor nothing, so it backs no recognition either. The hours are the hours that were booked, one credit each, not the minutes the call lasted: that is what the tutor was paid for.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.NotAParticipant
comment:
Somebody who is neither the student nor the tutor of a session asked for it.

Refused whatever they hold, a link included: the backend guide says only participants may read a session, and the room name is what lets anyone into the call.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.ParticipantRole
comment: Which of the two people of a session somebody is.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.Participation
comment:
One participant's presence in a session: that they came, as whom, and when they first did.

Written the first time they join and never duplicated, as {@code uq_participations_session_user} insists: a participant whose connection drops and comes back is still one participant, and {@code joined_at} keeps the first arrival, which is what punctuality is judged by. {@code end_confirmed_at} records whether, and when, they confirmed the end.

methods.name: arrived
methods.comment: A participant arriving for the first time.

methods.name: confirmEnd
methods.comment:
The participant says the session is over (US11).

Saying it again keeps the first time: it is the moment they declared the end, and a retried request must not move it.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.PresenceCheck
comment:
One participant's presence code in one session, and whether they typed it in (US54).

The code is emailed and only its hash is kept, salted with the check's id so two participants who happen to get the same six digits do not share a hash. Six digits are few, so the hash alone would not stop somebody reading the database from finding the code; what keeps the check honest is that the code expires within minutes and is dead after {@link #MAX_ATTEMPTS} wrong tries.

methods.name: newCode
methods.comment: Six random digits, leading zeros included.

methods.name: confirm
methods.comment:
The participant types the code in.

Typing it again once confirmed changes nothing, so a double click or a retried request does not spend an attempt. A wrong code spends one, and the caller must keep that attempt even though the answer is a refusal: otherwise the cap would never be reached.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.PresenceCheckUnavailable
comment:
Presence cannot be confirmed right now, whatever code is typed: no code has been issued yet, it expired, its attempts are spent, the participant never joined, or the session is no longer in progress.

A well formed request the state of the check refuses, which is why it answers 409 and not 400.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.domain.model.Session

The live meeting a confirmed booking turns into.

It is born scheduled, when booking announces the confirmation, and keeps only the booking's id: what the student needs help with belongs to the booking and is read from there.

methods.comment:
Lets a participant into the room.

The room opens {@link #JOIN_OPENS_BEFORE} before the start and closes at the scheduled end. The first participant to join starts the session, whoever it is: from then on it is in progress, and the start is when somebody actually arrived, not when it was scheduled. Joining a session already in progress changes nothing, so coming back after a dropped connection works.

Which one it is decides whether the tutor is paid, so the caller has to say it; the session only makes sure it is closed once.  @throws IllegalStateException when the session is not in progress

name: pe.ayni.sessions.infrastructure.PresenceCheckJob
comment:
Sends the presence codes of the sessions that reached their fifth minute, one university at a time.

Nobody makes this request, so each university is bound explicitly before anything is read, as the expired holds sweep does. It runs every minute because the code is due five minutes into an hour: a nightly job would be far too late. A session that fails is logged and tried again on the next run; the others are not held back by it.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

A participant's code, locked until the transaction ends.

For typing it in: without the lock, several wrong codes sent at once would each read the same count of attempts and the cap could be passed by guessing in parallel.

comment:
Closes the sessions nobody closed, fifteen minutes after their booked hour, one university at a time.

Runs every minute, like the presence codes: the tutor is paid when the session closes, and waiting for a nightly run would leave them unpaid for a day. A session that fails is logged and tried again on the next run; the others are not held back by it.

name: pe.ayni.sessions.infrastructure.SessionRepository

The sessions.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

A session, locked until the transaction ends.

For joining: the student and the tutor usually arrive within seconds of each other, and both could otherwise read the session as not started and both start it. The lock makes the second one wait and find it in progress.

The live session, for its two participants.

comment:
Maps the session's refusals and invalid HTTP input to the common error shape: timestamp, status, error, message, path.

403 for somebody who does not belong to the session, 409 for a participant arriving when the room is not open or confirming presence when it cannot be confirmed, 422 for a presence code that is well formed but wrong, 404 for a session the university does not have. Scoped to this module's controller, like every module's handler.

methods.comment: Six digits, just not the right ones: told apart from a malformed code, which is 400.

name: pe.ayni.shared.domain.CreditType
comment:
Origin of a group of credits.

The distinction carries the central rule of the product, and it is written here once so that no module has to remember it: only credits earned by teaching count towards recognition, and they are the only ones that never expire.

methods.name: expires
methods.comment: Whether credits of this type have an expiry date. Only what the university grants does.

methods.name: countsTowardsRecognition
methods.comment: Whether credits of this type count towards academic recognition.

name: pe.ayni.shared.domain.Credits
comment:
A whole amount of credits. One credit represents one hour of tutoring.

It is a type of its own rather than an {@code int} so that minutes, credits and money cannot be passed in place of one another by mistake: the compiler catches it.

Credits are never fractional, so the amount is an {@code int} and not a decimal. Instances are immutable, and the constructor rejects negatives, so an invalid amount cannot exist anywhere in the program.
