methods.comment: Subtracts the given amount.  @throws IllegalArgumentException when the result would be negative

methods.name: isGreaterThanOrEqualTo
methods.comment: Reads as the business rule it represents: whether a balance covers a price.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.AccessRequested
comment:
Published by identity when somebody asks for a single use access link.

It carries the link itself because notifications has to deliver it and identity only stores its hash. Events are held in memory today; if they are ever persisted, this one must not be stored with the link in clear.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.AvailabilityPublished
comment: Published by booking when a tutor saves or changes their weekly availability.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.BookingCancelled
comment:
Published by booking when a reservation is cancelled.

Cancelling always refunds, so wallet reacts to every one of these. {@code late} says whether it happened within twelve hours of the start, which booking records against whoever cancelled. Matching offers the released blocks again.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.BookingCancelled$CancelledBy
comment: Who cancelled. {@code SYSTEM} covers a session that ended unverified.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.BookingConfirmed
comment:
Published by booking once the credits were charged and the hours reserved, in the same transaction.

Sessions creates the session, matching removes the blocks from the search, notifications tells both participants.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.CoordinatorActivated
comment: Published by identity when an invited coordinator follows their link for the first time.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.CreditsExpired
comment: Published by wallet when unspent credits reach their expiry and leave the balance.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.CreditsExpiring
comment: Published by wallet ahead of the expiry of a group of credits, so the student can use them.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.CreditsGranted
comment: Published by wallet when credits arrive in an account.

comment:
Contract for every event published by one module and consumed by another.

Events live here, and not inside the module that publishes them, so that neither side depends on the other: both depend on this package. If {@code SessionCompleted} lived in {@code sessions}, then {@code wallet} would have to depend on {@code sessions} just to listen to it.

Every event states which university it belongs to, because whoever reacts to it runs outside the original request and has no other way of knowing.

methods.name: tenantId
methods.comment: University that owns the aggregate the event originated from.

methods.name: occurredOn
methods.comment: Moment the event happened, in UTC.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.HoursGenerated
comment:
Published by booking when new one hour blocks become available for a tutor.

Matching adds one offer per block and per skill the tutor has enabled.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.HoursGenerated$Block
comment: One generated hour.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.HoursWithdrawn
comment:
Published by booking when available blocks stop being offered: the tutor removed availability, paused, or the blocks were released without a booking.

Blocks taken by a booking are announced by {@link BookingConfirmed}, not here.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.PresenceCodeIssued
comment:
Published by sessions five minutes into a session, once per participant.

It carries the code in clear because notifications has to email it and sessions only stores its hash. The same warning as {@link AccessRequested} applies if events are ever persisted.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.PurchaseConfirmed
comment: Published by payments once the provider confirms a purchase, exactly once per purchase thanks to its idempotency key. Wallet credits the purchased credits.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.RecognitionRequested
comment: Published by recognition when a student submits a request to their university.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.RecognitionResolved
comment: Published by recognition when a coordinator approves or rejects a request, always with a reason.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SessionCompleted
comment:
Published by sessions when a session ends and both participants passed the presence check.

Several modules react: wallet credits the tutor with earned credits, reputation opens the rating window, recognition advances the progress and notifications tells both participants. None of them is named here, which is the point: a new consequence is a new listener, not a change to the code that closes a session.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SessionRated
comment:
Published by reputation when a participant rates a session.

Matching reacts to a student's rating by refreshing the tutor's standing in its projection, asking reputation for the new figures.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SessionRated$Direction
comment: Who rated whom.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SessionStarted
comment: Published by sessions when the first participant joins.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SessionUnverified
comment:
Published by sessions when a session ends without every participant confirming presence.

The tutor earns nothing, wallet refunds the student and audit records the failed check.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SkillEnabled
comment: Published by skills when a tutor becomes enabled to teach a catalogue item, by either path.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.SkillWithdrawn
comment: Published by skills when a tutor stops offering a catalogue item. Confirmed bookings stand.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.StudentActivated
comment:
Published by identity when a student enters for the first time and their academic profile has been imported.

Wallet reacts by granting the university's credits, and skills by enabling the courses the student's grades already justify.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.UniversityRegistered
comment: Published by identity when the platform administrator opens a new university.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.UniversitySuspended
comment: Published by identity when a university is suspended.

name: pe.ayni.shared.events.ValidationResolved
comment: Published by skills when a coordinator approves or rejects the evidence for a global tool.

name: pe.ayni.shared.tenancy.CurrentUser
comment:
Holds the person the request being processed on the current thread is about.

The companion of {@link TenantContext}: that one answers which university, this one answers who. Both are bound by a filter in {@code config}, so that a use case can ask for either without receiving it as a parameter through every method call.

The value arrives in the {@code X-User-Id} header today, exactly as the university arrives in {@code X-Tenant-Id}. When sign in is added it will come from a claim of the access token and only the filter changes.

Until then anyone can claim to be anybody, and that is precisely why an endpoint reads its subject from here rather than taking it as a parameter: an endpoint that has no way to name another student cannot be pointed at one, so the hole stays in one place instead of in every controller.

methods.name: set
methods.comment: Binds a user to the current thread.

methods.name: get
methods.comment: Returns the user bound to the current thread, or {@code null} when none is bound.

methods.name: require

comment:
Holds the university that owns the request being processed on the current thread.

Every university is a separate tenant. {@code TenantFilter} reads it from the request and pushes it here, so that a use case can ask for it without receiving it as a parameter through every method call.

Queries filter by this value today. Later the database will enforce the same thing by itself, and when that happens this class stays as it is.

methods.name: set
methods.comment: Binds a tenant to the current thread.

methods.name: get
methods.comment: Returns the tenant bound to the current thread, or {@code null} when none is bound.

methods.name: require
methods.comment: Returns the tenant bound to the current thread.  @throws MissingTenantException when no tenant is bound

methods.name: clear
methods.comment: Clears the tenant. Called when the request finishes, to avoid leaking across threads.

name: pe.ayni.skills.CatalogItemView
comment: A catalogue item as the other modules see it.

name: pe.ayni.skills.CatalogScope
comment: Global tools ship with Ayni; university courses belong to the university that teaches them.

name: pe.ayni.skills.SkillsApi
comment:
What skills offers to the other modules.

Implemented by a class in {@code skills.application}.

methods.name: isTutorEnabledFor
methods.comment: Whether the tutor is enabled, by grade or by reviewed evidence, to teach the item.

methods.name: enabledSkillsOf
methods.comment: Catalogue items the tutor is currently enabled to teach.

methods.name: requireItem
methods.comment: @throws java.util.NoSuchElementException when the item is not visible to the current tenant

methods.name: declareLearningInterests
methods.comment: Registers catalogue items a student needs help with, for US40's initial configuration. Declaring the same item twice is harmless.

methods.name: declareTeachingInterests
methods.comment:
Enables, by academic record, every item among these the student's approved courses already clear, for the "can teach" half of US40's initial configuration.

An item already offered, not backed by an approved course, or not a university course at all is skipped rather than refused, so a caller resuming an interrupted configuration does not need to filter the list first.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.CatalogQuery
comment: What a student of the current tenant may browse: the global items plus their own university's.

methods.name: visibleItems
methods.comment: One page of the active items visible to the current university, sorted by name.

methods.name: namePattern
methods.comment: A {@code LIKE} pattern that treats the student's text literally, wildcards included.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.DeclareInterestsUseCase
comment:
US40: the two halves of a student's initial configuration that belong to skills.

"Need help with" registers an interest of its own, {@link LearningInterest}. "Can teach" declares no interest: it goes straight through {@link OfferApprovedCourseUseCase}, the same academic-record path US13 built, since offering a course during onboarding is not a different operation from offering it from its own screen.

methods.name: declareLearningInterests
methods.comment:
Registers the items as courses the student needs help with. Repeats are harmless.

Every item must be visible to the student's university: the foreign key only proves the item exists, and would accept a course of another university. @throws NoSuchElementException when an item does not exist or belongs to another university

methods.name: declareTeachingInterests
methods.comment:
Enables, by academic record, every item among these the student's approved courses already clear.

An item already offered, not backed by an approved course, or not a university course at all is skipped rather than refused: US40 scenario 5 lets a student resume an interrupted configuration, and a second submission of the same choices must not fail on what the first one already did.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.OfferApprovedCourseUseCase
comment:
US13: offers a university course a tutor already passed, enabled the moment the grade clears the university's threshold.

Only university courses go through this path: a global tool has no academic record to check against, and reaches {@link pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.OfferedSkillStatus#ENABLED} only through reviewed evidence, which this use case does not build.

{@code identity} is injected {@code @Lazy}: identity has no implementation yet, and without it a plain injection would refuse to create this bean, which would in turn stop every other module's Spring context from starting, including tests that have nothing to do with skills. The proxy defers that lookup to the first call of {@link #execute}, so the rest of the application boots normally and only offering a skill fails until identity exists. Drop {@code @Lazy} once it does.

methods.name: execute
methods.comment: @throws NoSuchElementException when the item does not exist or is not visible to this tenant @throws SkillsRuleViolation when the item is retired or not a university course, the tutor's record has no matching approved course, the grade does not reach the university's threshold, or the tutor already offers it

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.SkillsService
comment:
What the other modules see of skills.

It holds no rules of its own: each answer is a read against this module's tables, and this class is the door the other modules are reached through. Matching depends on {@link SkillsApi} and never learns that {@code OfferedSkill} exists, so the inside of skills can be rearranged without anybody else changing.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.SuggestedCoursesQuery
comment:
US13, scenario 2: courses the tutor's academic record already clears, so they can be offered without the tutor having to search for them.

A course is suggested only when offering it would succeed: it is an active course of the university, its grade reaches the university's threshold, and the tutor has not offered it before (enabled, pending or even withdrawn), since {@link OfferApprovedCourseUseCase} refuses a second offer of the same item.

The answer costs the same whatever the length of the academic record: one read of the matching courses and one of the tutor's offers, instead of two queries per approved course.

{@code identity} is injected {@code @Lazy}, for the same reason as in {@link OfferApprovedCourseUseCase}: identity has no implementation yet, and a plain injection would stop every other module's Spring context from starting.

name: pe.ayni.skills.application.SuggestedCoursesQuery$SuggestedCourse
comment: A catalog item the tutor could offer, with the grade that would enable it.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.AccreditationPath
comment: How an offered skill reached {@link OfferedSkillStatus#ENABLED}.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.CatalogItem
comment:
Something a tutor can offer: a university course or a global tool, told apart by {@link #scope}.

Global tools ship with Ayni and are the same everywhere; university courses belong to the university that teaches them and carry the course code its academic system reports. A global item can never belong to a university, which would quietly make it invisible to every other one: {@link #validateInvariants()} enforces the same rule {@code ck_catalog_items_tenant_matches_scope} enforces in the database.

methods.name: retire
methods.comment: Retired items stop being offerable, but keep the history that already points at them.

methods.name: isVisibleTo
methods.comment: Whether a student of {@code tenantId} may see this item: it is global or their own.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.CatalogItemStatus
comment: Whether an item can currently be offered or accredited.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.Category
comment:
A group catalog items are organised under: technology, university courses, languages, design.

Global, the same for every university. Nothing in this module's scope creates one yet; they ship with Ayni and are seeded directly in the database.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.LearningInterest
comment:
What a student wants to receive help with, catalogue item by catalogue item.

Drives the recommendations shown on the portal. Declaring one twice for the same item is not an error, just a fact the database already knows: {@code uq_learning_interests_student_item} makes a repeat insert redundant rather than wrong, which is why nothing here refuses it.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.OfferedSkill
comment:
What a tutor is enabled to teach.

A university course reaches {@link OfferedSkillStatus#ENABLED} on its own when the grade clears the university's threshold ({@link #enableByAcademicRecord}, US13). A global tool can only reach it through reviewed evidence, because no academic record can vouch for it; that path is not built by this class yet.

methods.name: enableByAcademicRecord
methods.signature: enableByAcademicRecord(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.util.UUID, java.math.BigDecimal, java.math.BigDecimal, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: Offers a university course the tutor's academic record already clears.

methods.name: withdraw
methods.comment: Stops the tutor from offering this skill; reservations already confirmed are unaffected.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.OfferedSkillStatus
comment: Where an offered skill is in its life.

name: pe.ayni.skills.domain.model.SkillsRuleViolation
comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked of it.

Skills throws this instead of {@code IllegalArgumentException} or {@code IllegalStateException} so that its refusals can be told apart from a programming mistake. The two look identical from outside and deserve opposite answers: a refusal is something the caller can act on, a mistake is something somebody has to fix.

A missing argument is not one of these. {@code Objects.requireNonNull} stays where it is, because a null that reached an entity is a bug and not a decision.

name: pe.ayni.skills.infrastructure.CatalogItemRepository
comment: Every method takes the university: a global item has no {@code tenant_id} to filter by, so "visible to this tenant" always means global-or-mine, never a plain equality.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndCourseCodeInAndStatus
methods.comment: The university's courses in the given status among the codes the academic system reports.

name: pe.ayni.skills.infrastructure.CategoryRepository
comment: Global, so unlike the rest of this module's repositories it does not filter by tenant.

name: pe.ayni.skills.infrastructure.DemoSkillsData
comment:
A catalogue to look at while nothing else fills it.

No story in this cycle creates a category or a global tool, and university courses will come from each institution's academic system, which the platform does not integrate with yet. Until then US13 would have nothing to offer, so under the {@code dev} profile the module fills a small catalogue: a few global tools and the courses of one university.

It lives here and not in a migration on purpose. A migration runs in every environment and can never be taken back; demonstration data belongs to the developer's machine only, the same way {@code DemoWalletData} does for wallet.

It runs once. A second start finds the categories already there and leaves them alone. The identifiers are fixed so that requests saved in Swagger or in the frontend keep working.

name: pe.ayni.skills.infrastructure.LearningInterestRepository
comment: Every method takes the university: no query here may cross into another one's students.

name: pe.ayni.skills.infrastructure.OfferedSkillRepository
comment: Every method takes the university: no query here may cross into another one's tutors.

methods.name: existsByTenantIdAndTutorIdAndCatalogItemIdAndStatus
methods.comment: Whether some tutor of this tenant is enabled to teach the item, for {@code SkillsApi}.

methods.name: findCatalogItemIds
methods.comment:
The catalogue items a tutor holds in the given status.

Written out because a derived query cannot select a single column: Spring Data ignores whatever sits between {@code find} and {@code By}, returns whole entities, and Hibernate refuses to hand them back as identifiers.

methods.name: findAllCatalogItemIds
methods.comment: Every catalogue item the tutor ever offered, whatever became of the offer.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.ApiError
comment:
The one shape every error of this API answers with.

Same five fields for every failure, so the web application has one thing to handle and not one per endpoint.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.CatalogItemResponse
comment: A catalogue item as the student sees it.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.CatalogPage
comment:
A page of the catalogue.

Described with its own fields rather than returned as a Spring {@code Page}, whose shape is an implementation detail of the framework, the same way wallet answers its movement history.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.OfferSkillRequest
comment: The catalogue item the tutor wants to offer.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.OfferedSkillResponse
comment: What a tutor is now enabled to teach, right after the offer went through.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.SkillsController
comment:
The catalogue, and offering a course from it.

The controller does exactly two things: it reads the request and it calls a use case. It never touches an entity or a repository, and it holds no transaction, so the rules stay where they can be tested without HTTP.

Every endpoint answers about the tutor making the request, read from {@link CurrentUser}, and none takes a tutor as a parameter: until sign in exists, an endpoint that could name another tutor could be pointed at one.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.SkillsExceptionHandler
comment:
Turns the exceptions of this module into answers.

It is declared for skills' controller alone, so each module keeps its own mapping: a refusal that means one thing here should not quietly acquire a status code decided elsewhere.

methods.name: handleNotFound
methods.comment: The catalogue item does not exist, or is not visible to the requesting university.

methods.name: handleSkillsRuleViolation
methods.comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked, such as a grade below the threshold.

Only skills' own refusals are answered here. {@code IllegalArgumentException} used to be mapped instead, which turned every programming mistake below the controller into a 400 and hid it: a bug that answers "bad request" is a bug nobody reports.

methods.name: handleMissingTenant
methods.comment: No university on the request: the header is missing.

methods.name: handleMissingUser
methods.comment: No tutor on the request: the header is missing, or not a readable identifier.

methods.name: handleMissingHeader
methods.comment: A header the endpoint needs was not sent.

methods.name: handleInvalidBody
methods.comment: A request body that failed `@Valid`, such as a missing `catalogItemId`.

methods.name: handleInvalidParameter
methods.comment: A path or query parameter outside what the endpoint accepts.

name: pe.ayni.skills.interfaces.rest.SuggestedCourseResponse
comment: A course the tutor's academic record already clears, ready to be offered.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.ChargeReceipt
comment: Proof that a booking was charged.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.CreditBalanceView
comment: What a user can spend right now. Expired credits are not included.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.InsufficientCreditsException
comment: Thrown when a charge exceeds the available balance. Carries how many credits are missing.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.WalletApi
comment:
What wallet offers to the other modules. Wallet is the only module that writes the ledger.

Implemented by a class in {@code wallet.application}.

methods.name: charge
methods.comment:
Charges a booking, spending first the credits closest to expiring.

Runs inside the caller's transaction: if the booking fails afterwards, the charge rolls back with it. @throws InsufficientCreditsException when the balance does not cover the amount

methods.name: refund
methods.comment: Returns the credits of a booking to the groups they came from, with the expiry they had.

methods.name: grant
methods.comment: Places credits in an account.

methods.name: earnedTotal
methods.comment: Every credit the user ever earned by teaching, spent or not.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.Accounts
comment:
Finds the credit account a use case is about to work on.

The university always comes from {@link TenantContext}, never from the caller: a use case that accepted a tenant as a parameter would be one refactoring away from reading another university's wallet.

methods.name: find
methods.comment: The account of a student, when they have one.

methods.name: openIfAbsent
methods.comment:
The account of a student, opened if this is the first time credits reach them.

Accounts are not created when a student joins, because nothing would distinguish an empty wallet from a wallet that does not exist. They appear the first time something is granted.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.ChargeCredits
comment:
Spends a student's credits on a booking.

Booking calls this while it is confirming a reservation, and it runs inside booking's transaction: if reserving the hours fails after the charge, the credits come back by themselves because nothing was committed. That is why charging is a call and not an event.

methods.name: charge
methods.comment: Takes the credits of a booking, from the groups closest to expiring.  @throws InsufficientCreditsException when the spendable groups do not cover the amount. The exception carries how many credits are missing, so booking can tell the student.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.ExpireCredits
comment:
Takes the credits that reached their expiry out of the wallets.

The balance already ignores them: it only counts groups that are still alive, so nothing is wrong with a balance between the moment credits die and the moment this runs. What this adds is the entry in the history, which is what tells a student that six credits expired on the fifteenth rather than leaving them to notice the total is smaller.

methods.name: universitiesWithCreditsToExpire
methods.comment:
The universities that have something to expire right now.

The job runs outside any request, so there is no university bound to ask for, and identity does not exist yet to list them. Wallet answers it from its own groups, which is enough and does not reach into another module. When identity arrives this becomes {@code IdentityApi.activeTenantCodes()}.

methods.name: forCurrentUniversity
methods.comment:
Expires everything overdue in the university bound to the current thread.

One transaction per university: a failure while expiring one of them leaves the others expired, instead of rolling back the whole night's work.

methods.name: announce
methods.comment: Tells whoever is interested, once per student rather than once per group.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.GrantCredits
comment:
Places credits in a student's account.

Every credit in the product arrives through here: the university's initial grant, a session taught, a purchase. Each arrival is a new group, never an addition to an existing one, because the group is what carries the origin and the expiry those credits were given with.

methods.name: grant
methods.comment: Grants credits of one origin, opening the account if the student did not have one.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.LedgerWriter
comment:
Appends movements to a university's ledger.

Everything that moves credits goes through here, which is what keeps the two properties of the ledger true: the entries of a university are numbered without gaps, and each one carries the hash of the one before it. Both depend on appending one writer at a time, which is why the first thing this does is take the university's turn.

It has no transaction of its own on purpose. It runs inside the transaction of the use case that called it, so the entries and the groups they describe are written together or not at all.

methods.name: append
methods.comment: Writes one movement down.

methods.name: append
methods.comment:
Writes several movements down, in the order they are given.

A charge that takes credits from three groups is three entries, one per group, because that is what lets a refund put every credit back where it came from.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.MovementHistoryQuery
comment:
Answers what happened to a student's credits.

The history is the ledger, read back. Expired credits are in it and stay in it: they no longer count towards the balance, but the student can still see the grant that arrived and the day it died.

methods.name: of
methods.signature: of(java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.LedgerReason, int, int)
methods.comment: A page of the history, newest first.

methods.name: describe
methods.comment: Adds to every entry the type and expiry of the group it moved credits in or out of.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.MovementView
comment:
One line of the history, as the student reads it.

It carries the type and expiry of the group the credits moved in or out of, because "two credits spent" means something different depending on whether they were about to expire.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.RefundBooking
comment:
Returns the credits of a cancelled booking, or of one whose session ended unverified.

The credits go back to the groups they were taken from, with the expiry those groups had. A booking cancelled the day before an initial grant dies gives back credits that die the next day, not fresh ones: otherwise booking and cancelling would be a way of renewing credits that were about to expire.

Cancelling always refunds, so this runs for every cancellation, including the ones booking records against whoever cancelled late. A session that failed the presence check refunds too: the tutor earns nothing for it, and the student is not charged for it either.

methods.name: refund
methods.comment:
Gives back what a booking took.

Does nothing when the booking was never charged, and nothing again when it was already refunded: cancellation and an unverified session arrive as events, and an event that is delivered twice must not pay twice.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.WalletBalanceQuery
comment:
Answers what a student holds.

The balance is computed from the groups on every read, and the read is what decides which of them are still alive, so a group that expired a minute ago stops counting without anything having run in between.

methods.name: of
methods.comment:
The balance of a student, broken down by where the credits came from.

A student nobody has granted anything to has an empty wallet, not a missing one: they are shown a balance of zero and how to obtain credits, which is what US23 asks for.

methods.name: earnedTotal
methods.comment:
Every credit the student ever earned by teaching, spent or not.

Recognition asks for this rather than for the balance: what backs a request is the teaching that happened, and spending those credits afterwards does not undo it.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.WalletEventListeners
comment:
What wallet does about things that happened elsewhere.

These are facts, not orders: sessions says a session ended and does not know that credits exist. Each listener is the whole of wallet's reaction to one fact, which is why adding a consequence later means adding a method here rather than editing the module that published it.

Every one of them binds the university from the event before doing anything. A listener runs after the original request is over, possibly on another thread, so the university it belongs to can only come from the event itself. That is why every event carries it.

methods.name: on
methods.comment:
A session ended with both participants verified: the tutor earns one credit per hour taught.

Earned credits never expire and are the only ones that count towards recognition, which is the reason the presence check exists at all. A session that ends unverified publishes {@code SessionUnverified} instead and nothing arrives here.

methods.name: on
methods.comment:
A booking was cancelled: cancelling always refunds.

Whether it was late, and who it counts against, is booking's business. Wallet returns the credits either way.

methods.name: on
methods.comment:
A session ended without every participant proving their presence: the tutor earns nothing and the student gets back what the booking took.

The student is not charged for an hour nobody can vouch for, whoever failed the check. Who that was is audit's business, and the event names them.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: A purchase was confirmed: the credits are placed, and they never expire.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.application.WalletService
comment:
What the other modules see of wallet.

It holds no rules of its own: each operation is one use case, and this class is the door they are reached through. Booking depends on {@link WalletApi} and never learns that {@code ChargeCredits} exists, so the inside of wallet can be rearranged without anybody else changing.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.Allocation
comment:
How many credits a single group contributes to an operation.

A charge of three credits may take two from the group expiring in October and one from the group expiring in December. Each of those pairs is an allocation, and each becomes one ledger entry, which is what lets a refund know where every credit came from.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.Balance
comment:
What a student can spend, worked out from their groups of credits.

This is derived, never stored. Asking the groups every time costs one indexed query and removes a whole class of bug: a balance column that disagrees with the history is possible, and once it happens there is no way to tell which of the two is right.

methods.name: from
methods.comment:
Derives the balance from the groups of an account.

Expired groups are left out: their credits are gone, even though their rows stay where they are and their expiry is still in the history.

methods.name: empty
methods.comment: The balance of a student who has never been granted anything.

methods.name: isEmpty
methods.comment: Whether there is nothing left to spend.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.Balance$Group
comment: A group of credits as the student sees it: how many are left and when they die.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.Balance$TypeBreakdown
comment: The credits of one origin, and the groups they sit in.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.CreditAccount
comment:
The credit account of one student at one university.

It holds no balance. The balance is the sum of what is left in the student's {@link CreditLot groups}, and it is computed on every read. A stored balance and a history of movements are two truths that drift apart on the first failed transaction, and the one that can be recomputed is the one that has to go.

methods.name: open
methods.comment: Opens the account a student did not have yet.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.CreditLot
comment:
A group of credits that arrived together, from the same origin and with the same expiry.

Credits are held in groups rather than as a number because the group is what carries the two facts that matter about a credit: where it came from and when it dies. Spending takes from the group closest to expiring, and a refund puts the credits back in the group they left, with the expiry they had. Neither rule can be expressed against a single balance.

methods.name: granted
methods.signature: granted(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, pe.ayni.shared.domain.Credits, pe.ayni.shared.domain.CreditType, java.time.Instant, pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.CreditSource, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant)
methods.comment: Places a new group of credits in an account.

methods.name: consume
methods.comment: Takes credits out of this group.  @throws IllegalArgumentException when the group does not hold that many

methods.name: restore
methods.comment:
Puts refunded credits back, never above what the group originally held.

A group can only ever give back what it gave, so a refund cannot be used to create credits. @throws CreditRuleViolation when the group did not give that many away

methods.name: expire
methods.comment: Empties the group because it reached its expiry.

methods.name: isExpiredAt
methods.comment: Whether the group had already died at the given moment.

methods.name: isSpendableAt
methods.comment: Whether the group still holds credits that can be spent right now.

methods.name: countsTowardsRecognition
methods.comment: Whether these credits count towards the recognition the university may grant.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.CreditRuleViolation
comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked of it.

Wallet throws this instead of {@code IllegalArgumentException} so that its refusals can be told apart from a programming mistake. The two look identical from outside and deserve opposite answers: a refusal is a 400 the caller can act on, a mistake is a 500 somebody has to fix.

{@code InsufficientCreditsException} is not one of these. It sits at the module root because booking catches it by name and shows the student how many credits they are short.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.CreditSource
comment:
What put a group of credits in an account.

The origin decides how the movement is written in the ledger, so the mapping lives here once instead of in every use case that grants credits.

methods.name: reason
methods.comment: How the arrival of these credits is recorded in the ledger.

methods.name: referenceType
methods.comment: What the ledger entry points at: the policy, the session, the purchase.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: The origin that grants credits of the given type.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.LedgerDirection
comment: Whether a movement took credits out of the account or put them in.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.LedgerEntry
comment:
One movement, written down for good.

Entries are never updated and never deleted: a mistake is answered with a new {@link LedgerReason#ADJUSTMENT} entry, and the mistake stays visible. A trigger in the database refuses {@code UPDATE} and {@code DELETE}, so this holds for anyone with a psql prompt too, not only for code that goes through this class.

Each entry carries the hash of the one before it, chained per university. Changing a row behind the application's back leaves its hash no longer matching its contents and breaks every link after it, which is what makes the tampering findable rather than merely forbidden.

methods.name: following
methods.comment: Writes a movement down as the next link of a university's chain.

methods.name: followingHash
methods.comment:
The same, when all that is known of the previous entry is its hash.

That is the case when appending: the tail of the chain is read as two columns under a lock, and loading the whole entry to take one field off it would buy nothing.

methods.name: computeHash
methods.comment:
Recomputes the hash from the fields as they stand now.

An entry whose stored hash no longer equals this was changed outside the application. Every column the entry owns goes in, {@code id} included: a row whose identifier was swapped for another is as tampered with as one whose amount was.

methods.name: matchesOwnHash
methods.comment: Whether the entry still matches its own hash.

methods.name: follows
methods.comment: Whether this entry follows the given one, which is {@code null} for the first of a chain.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.LedgerReason
comment:
Why a movement happened.

The ledger is append only, so a mistake is not edited away: it is answered with a new {@link #ADJUSTMENT} entry that says what the correction is and leaves the mistake visible.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.Movement
comment:
What happened to an account, before it is written down.

A movement is the business fact: these credits left that group, for this reason. The {@link LedgerEntry} is the same fact once it has taken its place in the chain, with a sequence number and a hash. Keeping them apart is what lets the rules be decided without knowing the position an entry will end up in.

methods.name: debit
methods.comment: Credits leaving the account.

methods.name: credit
methods.comment: Credits arriving in the account.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.model.ReferenceType
comment:
What a ledger entry points at outside wallet.

Only the identifier is kept, never a foreign key: the booking, the session and the purchase belong to other modules and other schemas. Whoever needs the rest asks that module for it.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.services.LedgerChain
comment:
Checks that a university's ledger is still the one the application wrote.

Two things are verified for every entry: that it matches its own hash, and that it carries the hash of the entry before it. The first catches a row edited in place; the second catches a row removed, inserted or reordered. A trigger already refuses {@code UPDATE} and {@code DELETE}, so this is what remains for the cases the trigger cannot see: a restore from a doctored backup, or a superuser who dropped the trigger first.

methods.name: firstTamperedEntry
methods.comment:
Returns the first entry that does not add up, if there is one.

The entries are verified in sequence order, so the answer is the point where the history stopped being trustworthy, not merely that something somewhere is wrong.

methods.name: isIntact
methods.comment: Whether the whole chain holds.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.services.RefundPlan
comment:
Which groups a refund returns credits to.

A refund is not "add the credits back". The credits go home: to the same groups they were taken from, with the expiry those groups had. Otherwise cancelling a booking would quietly launder credits that were about to die into credits that live longer, and a student could keep an expiring grant alive by booking and cancelling.

The ledger is what remembers where they came from, which is the whole reason a charge writes one entry per group instead of a single total.

methods.name: of
methods.comment:
Works out what a booking owes back, from the entries it left in the ledger.

Refunds already given are subtracted, so refunding twice returns nothing the second time. Cancelling is announced by an event, and an event that arrives twice must not pay twice.

methods.name: isEmpty
methods.comment: Whether there is nothing left to return, because it was refunded already.

methods.name: total
methods.comment: The credits this plan returns.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.domain.services.SpendingPlan
comment:
Which groups a charge takes its credits from.

The rule is one line and it is the reason this class exists: spend first what expires first. A student holding credits that die in October and credits that never die should not lose the October ones while the others sit untouched.

Nothing here touches the database or the clock: it is given the groups, the amount and the moment, and it answers where the credits come from. That is what makes the rule testable without starting Spring.

methods.name: of
methods.comment:
Works out which groups pay for the given amount.

Groups that already expired are not considered, however many credits they still hold: an expired credit is gone even though its row is still there for the history to show. @throws InsufficientCreditsException when the spendable groups do not add up to the amount, carrying how many credits are missing

methods.name: total
methods.comment: The credits this plan spends, which always equals the amount it was asked for.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.CreditAccountRepository
comment:
Credit accounts.

Every method takes the university: until the database enforces the separation by itself, a query without that filter reads another university's data.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndIdIn
methods.comment: The given accounts, for turning account identifiers back into students.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.CreditExpiryJob
comment:
Runs the expiry once a night, university by university.

The job holds no rule: it decides when, and {@code ExpireCredits} decides what. It binds the university before calling, exactly as {@code TenantFilter} does for a request, so that a use case reads it from {@link TenantContext} without caring whether it was started by a student or by the clock.

Each university is a call of its own, and therefore a transaction of its own: one that fails does not take the others with it.

methods.name: expireOverdueCredits
methods.comment: Every night at three, when nobody is booking anything.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.CreditLotRepository
comment:
Groups of credits.

Two of these queries take a write lock. Credits are the one thing in this product that can be spent twice if two requests read the same groups at the same time, and the groups carry no version column, so the rows are locked while they are being spent.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndAccountId
methods.comment: Every group of an account, spent or not, expired or not: the history needs all of them.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndIdIn
methods.comment: The given groups, for a read that is not about to change them.

methods.name: lockByIds
methods.comment: The given groups, locked, for a refund that is about to put credits back in them.

methods.name: lockSpendable
methods.comment:
The groups a charge may take from, locked until the transaction ends.

They come back unordered on purpose: the order credits are spent in is a rule of the product, and it belongs in {@code SpendingPlan} where it can be read and tested, not in an {@code ORDER BY} that nobody reviews.

methods.name: lockExpired
methods.comment: The groups that have reached their expiry with credits still in them.

methods.name: tenantsWithCreditsToExpire
methods.comment:
The universities that have credits to expire.

The scheduled job runs outside any request, so there is no tenant bound to ask for. When identity exists this becomes {@code IdentityApi.activeTenantCodes()}; until then wallet can answer it from its own data without reaching into another module.

methods.name: sumOriginalAmount
methods.comment:
Everything the student was ever granted of one type, spent or not.

Recognition asks for the earned total, and what backs a recognition request is the teaching that happened, not what is left in the wallet afterwards.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.DemoWalletData
comment:
Two wallets to look at while identity does not exist.

Nothing grants credits today: the university's policy arrives with {@code StudentActivated}, which identity will publish. Until then the endpoints would answer an empty wallet to everyone and there would be nothing to review, so under the {@code dev} profile the module fills two accounts that between them show everything US23 asks for.

It is written through the published interface and the real use cases, never with direct inserts: demonstration data that took a shortcut the application cannot take is data that proves nothing. The expiries below are produced by running the real expiry.

It runs once. A second start finds the accounts already there and leaves them alone, so restarting the backend does not double anybody's credits.

methods.name: inDays
methods.comment:
A whole day away, at midnight UTC.

A credit policy expires on a date, not at whatever time of day the container happened to start, and a round date is easier to read in Swagger.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.LedgerEntryRepository
comment: The ledger. Entries are inserted and read, never changed: the entity is immutable and a trigger refuses {@code UPDATE} and {@code DELETE} in the database.

methods.name: lockLedgerOf
methods.comment:
Takes this university's turn to append, and holds it until the transaction ends.

This is what makes the chain a chain. Without it, two transactions appending at once read the same tail, claim the same sequence number, and one of them is rejected by {@code uq_ledger_entries_sequence} after having done all of its work.

Locking the last row instead is the obvious thing to do, and it does not work. PostgreSQL re-checks the row a blocked transaction was waiting on, but it does not re-run the {@code order by ... limit 1} that chose it, so the second writer wakes up still believing the old tail is the tail. An advisory lock has no row to go stale: it is held on the university itself, so the writers really do queue, and it covers the first entry of a university, when there is no row to lock at all.

Two universities whose codes happen to hash alike queue behind each other. That costs a little waiting and is never wrong, which is the right way round for this trade.

methods.name: chainTailOf
methods.comment:
Where a university's chain currently ends.

Only ever read after {@link #lockLedgerOf(String)}, which is what keeps the answer true for as long as it takes to use it. Two columns are enough: appending needs the number to continue from and the hash to point at.

methods.name: findByTenantIdAndReferenceTypeAndReferenceIdOrderBySequenceNumberAsc
methods.comment: Everything ever written about one thing outside wallet, such as a booking.

methods.name: findHistory
methods.signature: findHistory(java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, java.util.Collection, org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable)
methods.comment:
The history of an account, newest first.

The period and the reasons are always given: the query service turns "no filter" into the widest period and every reason, which keeps one query instead of one per combination of filters.

methods.name: findByTenantIdOrderBySequenceNumberAsc
methods.comment: Every entry of a university, in order, for verifying the chain.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.LedgerEntryRepository$ChainTail
comment: The last link of a chain: what to continue from.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.infrastructure.WalletSchedulingConfig
comment:
Turns on Spring's scheduler, which wallet needs for the nightly expiry.

It lives here rather than in {@code config} because wallet is the only module that schedules anything today. Another module declaring the same annotation changes nothing: it registers the same scheduler once. If scheduled work becomes common, this moves to {@code config} and this class disappears.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.ApiError
comment:
The one shape every error of this API answers with.

Same five fields for every failure, so the web application has one thing to handle and not one per endpoint.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.MovementsPage
comment:
A page of the credit history.

The page is described with its own fields rather than returned as a Spring {@code Page}, whose shape is an implementation detail of the framework and changes between versions. What the API promises should not.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.MovementsPage$Movement
comment: One movement.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.WalletBalanceResponse
comment: The balance as US23 asks for it: the total, where it came from, and when each part dies.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.WalletBalanceResponse$Group
comment: A group of credits that arrived together.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.WalletBalanceResponse$TypeBalance
comment: The credits of one origin.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.WalletController
comment:
What a student can ask about their own credits.

The controller does exactly two things: it reads the request and it calls a use case. It never touches an entity or a repository, and it holds no transaction, so the rules stay where they can be tested without HTTP.

Both endpoints answer about the student making the request, read from {@link CurrentUser}, and neither takes a student as a parameter. That is deliberate: until sign in exists, an endpoint that could name another student could be pointed at one.

name: pe.ayni.wallet.interfaces.rest.WalletExceptionHandler
comment:
Turns the exceptions of this module into answers.

It is declared for wallet's controller alone, so each module keeps its own mapping: a refusal that means one thing here should not quietly acquire a status code decided elsewhere.

methods.name: handleInsufficientCredits
methods.comment:
Not enough credits.

409 and not 400: the request was perfectly well formed, it is the state of the wallet that refuses it. The message carries how many credits are missing.

methods.name: handleMissingTenant
methods.comment: No university on the request: the header is missing.

methods.name: handleMissingUser
methods.comment: No student on the request: the header is missing, or not a readable identifier.

methods.name: handleMissingHeader
methods.comment: A header the endpoint needs was not sent.

methods.name: handleUnreadableParameter
methods.comment: A date, a user or a reason that could not be read.

methods.name: handleInvalidParameter
methods.comment: A page or a size outside what the endpoint accepts.

methods.name: handleCreditRuleViolation
methods.comment:
A rule of this module refusing what was asked, such as a charge of zero credits.

Only wallet's own refusals are answered here. {@code IllegalArgumentException} used to be mapped instead, which turned every programming mistake below the controller into a 400 and hid it: a bug that answers "bad request" is a bug nobody reports.
